name: Fiscal populism
summary: Fiscal populism favours higher government spending and tax cuts to win or hold votes in the short term, while downplaying fiscal conservatism, long-term budget sustainability and austerity. It is a budget style more than a full worldview, and economists such as Dornbusch and Edwards describe similar programmes as putting growth and distribution ahead of inflation, deficits and external limits.
scope: The strand described in the Wikipedia article on fiscal populism and the Dornbusch and Edwards account of macroeconomic populism in Latin America (Allende's Chile, Garcia's Peru), with Peron's Twenty Truths as a primary example of the social-justice side. It covers budget and macroeconomic stance only, so most social, cultural and foreign-policy statements are answered neutral with low confidence. Note that the label is often applied by critics rather than adopted by adherents.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Inferred from the approach's preference for voter-friendly public benefits; the sources do not name healthcare.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Inferred from Dornbusch and Edwards' account of populists putting income distribution ahead of inflation; the minimum wage is not named.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The populist macro programme relies on state-directed demand and non-market measures, though it is a budget style rather than a stated theory of markets.

public-ownership.rationale: Left versions of economic populism back public ownership, but right-leaning fiscal populists (tax-cut platforms) do not, so the label itself takes no side.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The Wikipedia article pairs spending with tax cuts, and critics have also used the label against a wealth tax; the ideology has no fixed line on taxing the rich.

unions-good.rationale: Wage-raising populist governments often court unions, but fiscal populism is defined by budget stance, not labour policy.

property-fundamental.rationale: Nothing in the definition of fiscal populism concerns property rights, so adherents differ by wider politics.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Left economic populists attack corporate power while tax-cutting fiscal populists court business; the label takes no common stand.

cut-welfare.rationale: Fiscal populism favours higher government spending and voter-friendly benefits, so cutting welfare is the austerity it opposes.

worker-ownership.rationale: Workplace ownership is a left-populist theme at most; fiscal populism as a budget style is silent on it.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Security policy lies outside what fiscal populism defines, so a committed adherent could go either way.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Drug policy is unrelated to the budget stance that defines the label.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Speech law is unrelated to fiscal populism's focus on spending and taxes.

strong-leader.rationale: Perón-style movements value a strong leader, but fiscal populists in parliamentary democracies such as Japan do not.

state-harmful.rationale: Fiscal populists want an active spending state that delivers benefits; abolishing it is the opposite of their programme.

limit-guns.rationale: Gun control has no link to the fiscal stance that defines the label.

empower-police-military.rationale: Some fiscal populists (Japan's DPP) back higher defence spending, but the label itself takes no stand on security.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: A social question outside the definition of fiscal populism.

decide-locally.rationale: The definition says nothing about decentralisation; populist movements range from centralist to local.

rehabilitation.rationale: Penal policy is outside what fiscal populism defines.

traditional-family.rationale: Family values are not part of fiscal populism, which is defined by budget policy.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Not addressed by a budget-focused label; adherents follow their wider politics.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed by a budget-focused label; adherents follow their wider politics.

more-religion-public.rationale: Religion's public role is outside the definition of fiscal populism.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: No documented link between fiscal populism and race policy; adherents vary.

gender-social-construct.rationale: A theoretical question unrelated to fiscal populism.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Cultural policy is outside the label; right and left populists differ.

gradual-change.rationale: Populists promise quick gains for voters and reject austerity-style gradual consolidation, so patience is not their style, though no source states this on social change.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The DPP flirted with immigrant-related proposals, but fiscal populism as a label has no immigration line.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Fiscal populists resist outside bodies that impose budget discipline, but the label does not address the UN-style question directly.

free-trade.rationale: Left economic populists distrust globalisation, while tax-cutting populists do not; there is no common position.

nation-first.rationale: The label concerns budgets, not foreign relations.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Foreign policy is outside fiscal populism.

open-borders.rationale: Populist movements generally stress the national community, but the budget-based label does not state a border policy.

limit-growth.rationale: Dornbusch and Edwards say the approach prizes growth, so a deliberate limit on growth contradicts it.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Climate policy is outside the definition; costs and spending appeal differ by faction.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Not related to fiscal populism's definition.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Japan's DPP backs nuclear restarts, but this reflects its energy policy rather than fiscal populism.

revolution-justified.rationale: Fiscal populism works through elections and budgets, but revolution is not discussed in the sources.

experts-over-public.rationale: Populism's anti-elitist stance suggests distrust of technocrats, though the sources on fiscal populism do not state it.

central-planning.rationale: Allende-era programmes leaned on state direction, whereas electoral tax-cut populists do not.

socialized-markets.rationale: No documented stance; the label concerns budgets rather than ownership.

land-value-tax.rationale: A tax shift that raises revenue to replace others cuts against the tax-cut appeal, but the source does not mention it.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not addressed; tax-cutting populists oppose it and redistributive ones favour it.

basic-income.rationale: A universal benefit fits populist spending, and Lee Jae-myung's minor basic income is cited as a populist measure, but it is not a defining demand.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Left populists often protect industry while others do not; the label has no fixed line.

state-directs-investment.rationale: State-led development appears in the Latin American populist cases, but the budget-focused label is not defined by it.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Inferred: the populist programme depends on money wages and real-wage growth, so abolishing them is opposed; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Populist governments tend to want central banks to serve fiscal goals, but they do not usually propose abolishing them.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Perón's movement favoured state-organised labour, but other fiscal populists do not.

one-party-rule.rationale: Fiscal populists in the Japanese example compete in multiparty elections; no source says they want a single party.

democracy-best.rationale: Inferred: the Wikipedia article describes fiscal populism as a vote-winning approach, which presumes competitive elections; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

direct-votes.rationale: Populists often like referendums, but the budget-based label does not require them.

workers-councils.rationale: Nothing links fiscal populism to council rule; it operates through parliaments and budgets.

natural-rulers.rationale: Anti-elitism makes this unlikely, but no source on fiscal populism discusses it.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Fiscal populists want a state that spends, so privatising core state functions is unlikely, though the sources do not discuss it.

military-superiority.rationale: Some adherents such as the DPP back defence spending, others do not.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Not addressed; right populists and left populists differ.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Perón rejected class conflict for national unity, and fiscal populism as a budget style takes no stand.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The approach stresses redistribution, but not full equality of outcomes.

self-interest-moral.rationale: A philosophical question outside fiscal populism.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Perón balanced individual rights against community needs, but fiscal populism proper takes no line.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Inferred: an approach built on growth and rising consumption holds the opposite view of industry; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Populists appeal to voter outcomes, but the label has no stand on pragmatism.

direct-action.rationale: Fiscal populism works through elections and budgets, though the sources do not discuss direct action.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Inferred: a growth and consumption approach rejects a return to hunter-gatherer life; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

distribute-by-need.rationale: The approach emphasises distribution, but no source says it adopts the communist principle of need.

profit-exploitation.rationale: A Marxist claim not adopted by the budget-based label.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Fiscal populists compete in elections; no source ties them to proletarian dictatorship.

taxation-theft.rationale: Fiscal populism needs taxation to fund benefits (and complains about its limits only through cuts), so it does not call tax theft.

exit-over-voice.rationale: The model depends on voting and elections, though the sources do not discuss exit.

state-as-business.rationale: Fiscal populism rejects running the state with business-style budget discipline, which is the nearest thing the label addresses.

positive-liberty.rationale: Not addressed by the label, though a benefits-heavy view would find it congenial.

media-academia-power.rationale: Populists often attack the media, but the label does not require it.

organic-representation.rationale: Peronism embraced corporatist representation; fiscal populism in general does not.

total-state.rationale: Fiscal populists in the Japanese example keep a pluralist democracy, but total state control is not discussed.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Not part of a vote-seeking fiscal style, though not discussed in the sources.

bound-labor.rationale: Inferred: rising wages and worker incomes are central; bound labour contradicts the programme; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

single-common-good.rationale: Perón's doctrine treats the nation's good as one aim, but fiscal populism as a label does not.

workplace-democracy.rationale: A left-populist theme at most; not a part of fiscal populism.

school-vouchers.rationale: No documented stance; vouchers are a spending choice some populists back and others oppose.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: The article defines fiscal populism as higher spending and tax cuts that downplay fiscal conservatism and budget sustainability, the opposite of avoiding deficits.

economic-freedom.rationale: Not addressed by the label; Perón's own doctrine subordinated capital to social welfare.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The Japanese DPP floated limits for foreign residents, but this is not a part of the label.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Voter-friendly benefits are central, so strict work tests are unlikely, but this is not stated in the sources.

class-collaboration.rationale: Perón sought national unity over class conflict, but fiscal populism as a label takes no stand.

workers-nation.rationale: Perón organised workers nationally, but the label itself does not require it.

ban-interest.rationale: Deficit-financed spending relies on borrowing, so banning interest is unlikely, though sources do not mention it.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Inferred: a vote-seeking approach aimed at broad popular benefit has no place for racial segregation by law; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy claim outside the label.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Populism of all kinds is anti-elitist, and the Wikipedia article on economic populism stresses opposition to the establishment, but this is not a fiscal-specific claim.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Inferred: a programme built on popular benefits has no basis for eugenic limits; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Fiscal populism is defined by expanding government spending and benefits, which a state limited to defence and justice would rule out.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Inferred: there is no basis for racial restrictions in a popular-benefits approach; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Peronist doctrine puts the common people first, but the label itself does not discuss equal rights.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Inferred: the Wikipedia article treats fiscal populism as an electoral strategy for winning votes, which presumes government by popular consent; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

trade-surplus.rationale: Populist programmes in the Latin American cases ran external deficits, but no source states a view on export targets.

population-transfer.rationale: Inferred: forced transfers have no role in a programme of popular benefits; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Not addressed; fiscal populists accept taxation, which libertarians call force.

separated-powers.rationale: Perón favoured a centralised government, while Japanese fiscal populists accept separated powers.

vanguard-party.rationale: Fiscal populists work through ordinary parties and elections; no source ties them to vanguard parties.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Dornbusch and Edwards describe distribution as a core aim of the approach, though it is mainly aimed at broad voter groups.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Not addressed; a popular giveaway some adherents might favour.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Wage-raising populist governments tend to side with workers, though the sources do not address strike law.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The approach blames lack of demand and distribution rather than population, but no source states it.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price controls are among the policies Dornbusch and Edwards associate with macroeconomic populist programmes.

party-controls-media.rationale: Japanese fiscal populists operate in a free-press democracy, though media control is not discussed in the sources.

party-commands-army.rationale: Not part of fiscal populism, which operates in electoral democracies.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Left populists sometimes favour pay caps for politicians, but the label does not.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Fiscal populists resist external fiscal limits, such as EU debt rules, but no source states it for this question.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Perón-style presidentialism favoured it, but the label does not.

clerical-rule.rationale: Fiscal populism is an electoral strategy and has no clerical element.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Perón's movement pushed for re-election, but other fiscal populists do not.

recall-officials.rationale: Populists often like recall, but the label does not require it.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: A radical measure beyond a benefits-and-tax-cut approach, though the sources do not discuss it.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Populist anti-elitism often includes this view, but it is not part of the fiscal label.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Populist governments facing external limits have resisted repaying foreign creditors, though the sources do not state this as a defining demand.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Perón's economic independence flag points that way, but fiscal populism as a label does not.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The label is about winning votes, which depends on political freedom, though the sources do not discuss the trade-off.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The approach prioritises growth and deficit financing over inflation concerns, which an independent price-stability central bank would resist.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Perón put capital in service of the economy and social welfare, but the fiscal label does not address property.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Inferred: an elected, vote-seeking style of politics has no place for sacred rulers; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax cuts feature in the definition, but the label does not specify a flat rate.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: The model works through elected governments, though the sources do not discuss rule of law.

leader-cult.rationale: Perón's movement had a leader cult, but fiscal populists in general do not.

land-redistribution.rationale: Left populists such as the EFF and ZANU-PF back it, whereas the fiscal label does not.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: A vote-seeking style does not support it, though the sources do not discuss it.

women-must-cover.rationale: Not part of a budget-focused label, though the sources do not discuss it.

common-currency.rationale: A shared currency removes control over deficit financing, which fiscal populists prize, though no source says it directly.

ban-cartels.rationale: Anti-monopoly sentiment is part of left populism, but the fiscal label does not require it.

no-bailouts.rationale: Fiscal populists spend freely for popular aims, but bank bailouts are unpopular with voters, so the sources give no clear line.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Populists often favour majority rule over courts, but the fiscal label does not.

moral-incentives.rationale: The approach relies on material gains for voters, though no source discusses moral incentives.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: The label is an electoral strategy and does not involve armed groups.

public-money-creation.rationale: Dornbusch and Edwards describe deficit financing through the central bank, which comes close to public money creation, but this is not a stated demand.

delink-world-market.rationale: The approach is an expansionary growth strategy that needs trade and credit, though it is not framed in these terms.

freedom-to-discriminate.rationale: Not addressed by the label; a mass-appeal approach would not stress it.

elective-rulers.rationale: Inferred: fiscal populism is described as a way to win votes, which assumes elected rulers; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

minority-veto.rationale: Populism favours majority will, but the sources do not address minority vetoes.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Perón's social assistance pillar suggests it, but the label does not.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Inferred: fiscal populism is a way of winning votes and holding power, so political abstention is the opposite; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Perón's economic independence flag points that way, but the fiscal label does not.

paid-care-work.rationale: A spending-friendly approach would fund it, though it is not a documented demand.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: Left economic populists distrust foreign capital, but the fiscal label does not.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Voter-friendly public benefits favour state pensions, though the sources do not discuss pension design.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Not addressed by the label, though fiscal populists in Japan act through the Diet.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: A programme built on boosting consumption and incomes does not treat it as harmful, though no source states this.

corporate-influence.rationale: Left populists attack lobbying, but tax-cut populists do not, so there is no shared line.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Family cash benefits fit a generous spending approach, but this is not a documented position.

job-guarantee.rationale: A job guarantee fits growth-and-employment aims, though the sources do not name it.

socialized-care.rationale: Public provision fits a spending-heavy approach, but this is not documented.

majority-settlement.rationale: Not part of a budget-focused label.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Perón's Justicialism claimed a third position, but the fiscal label does not.

holocaust-denial.rationale: Inferred: there is no basis for it in a vote-seeking economic approach; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Fiscal populism needs elections to work, though the sources do not discuss repression.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Populists often claim to be beyond left and right, but fiscal populism is a budget style that varies by party.

social-market-economy.rationale: Not addressed by the label as such; the approach favours more spending than most social-market models.

rich-first.rationale: The approach stresses direct distribution to broad groups, though no source discusses trickle-down.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Dornbusch and Edwards describe populist governments as ignoring external constraints and resisting austerity, which matches rejecting lender conditions.

property-franchise.rationale: Inferred: a strategy built on winning mass votes cannot restrict the franchise by wealth; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

racial-franchise.rationale: Inferred: a strategy built on winning mass votes cannot restrict the franchise by race; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Not part of a budget-focused label.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Left populists say so, whereas tax-cutting fiscal populists do not.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Fiscal populism emphasises state benefits, though the sources do not discuss charities.

rent-control.rationale: Price controls are a populist staple in the Dornbusch and Edwards account, which suggests rent caps, though rent is not discussed.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Perón's doctrine honoured labour, but the fiscal label does not.

local-essentials-public.rationale: State-led provision of essentials fits the approach, but the sources do not discuss water or hospitals.

family-wage.rationale: Wage-raising aims fit a family-sized wage, though it is not a stated demand.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Perón rooted Justicialism in Christian values, but the fiscal label does not.

free-public-college.rationale: Free tuition is a typical voter-friendly benefit, but it is not a documented demand.

pollution-taxes.rationale: New taxes on consumers run against the tax-cut appeal, though the sources do not discuss them.

future-generations.rationale: Fiscal populism concerns budgets and deficits; it takes no position on handing on the Earth undamaged, and the article's "long-term sustainability" is fiscal, not environmental.

capital-controls.rationale: Populist programmes meeting external constraints often turn to controls, but the abstract does not mention them.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: A benefit and tax-cut approach fits it, but it is not a documented demand.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: The article says fiscal populism downplays fiscal conservatism and long-term budget sustainability, so binding rules that limit borrowing are what it rejects.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Inferred: fiscal populism wants to use the state's budget to deliver benefits, not destroy it; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Inferred from the approach's preference for popular spending measures; the article gives no student-debt example.

farm-price-support.rationale: Guaranteed prices fit a price-control and support approach, but farms are not discussed.

women-suffrage.rationale: Inferred: a vote-seeking approach seeks the whole electorate, so it supports equal suffrage; the sources cover budget policy only and do not address this.

indirect-election.rationale: A vote-winning approach favours direct popular elections, though sources do not discuss indirect election.

simple-living.rationale: A programme aimed at raising consumption and growth does not praise frugality, though sources do not discuss it.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Social cohesion and diversity lie outside a budget-focused label; right and left populists take opposite sides.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Religious doctrine is outside the definition of fiscal populism, which is about spending and taxes.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Japan's DPP proposed halving the consumption tax and Reiwa Shinsengumi proposed abolishing it, as the Wikipedia article reports.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Fiscal populism covers budget stance only, so it takes no position here.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Outside the budget focus of the ideology, so neutral is inferred.

close-ties-china.rationale: Outside the budget focus of the ideology, so neutral is inferred.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Outside the budget focus of the ideology, so neutral is inferred.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Outside the budget focus; left and right fiscal populists would differ.

self-ownership.rationale: Outside the budget focus of the ideology, so neutral is inferred.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Inferred from its vote-winning, broad benefits; Peron's Twenty Truths stress social welfare for all, but targeting is not discussed.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Some populists bypass parties, but this is a budget style rather than a view of representation.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Outside the budget focus; sources do not say whether favoured firms are accepted.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Outside the budget focus of the ideology, so neutral is inferred.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: Outside the budget focus of the ideology, so neutral is inferred.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Outside the budget focus of the ideology, so neutral is inferred.

national-resource-control.rationale: Inferred from Latin American cases such as Allende and Peron, which stressed national economic control; not part of the budget definition.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Inferred from Dornbusch and Edwards' account of populists putting income distribution ahead of other limits, which favours outcome over process.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Not addressed; the approach is about spending and tax cuts, not financial levies.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Not addressed; the label covers budget style only.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Not addressed; the label covers budget style only.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Not addressed; populist programmes have no stated view on automation.

multipolar-world.rationale: Not addressed; the label covers budget style only.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Not addressed in the macroeconomic account; no stance on value theory is inferred.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Inferred from the Peronist example, where the Twenty Truths join national sovereignty with social justice for workers.

material-over-identity.rationale: Not addressed; the label covers budget style only.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Not addressed; the label covers budget style only.

missingStatements.text: Governments should cut taxes and raise spending to boost the economy, even if that means larger deficits.
missingStatements.rationale: This is the defining position of fiscal populism, which the existing deficit statement only covers from the opposing side.

missingStatements.text: A government should not impose spending cuts or tax rises to reduce its debt.
missingStatements.rationale: The article describes fiscal populism as the opposite of austerity, which it contrasts with budget consolidation.

missingStatements.text: Consumption or sales taxes on everyday goods should be cut or abolished.
missingStatements.rationale: Japan's DPP proposed halving the consumption tax and Reiwa Shinsengumi proposed abolishing it, as the Wikipedia article reports.

notes: Fiscal populism is often a charge made by critics (for example Spanish and Japanese politicians) rather than a self-description, and it appears on both left and right. The profile is therefore thin outside budget questions.
